what: MIT's START went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions from the public on many topics (Boris Katz)
fit: A publicly reachable computer answering ordinary-language factual questions on many topics, used by outside people for that purpose; knowledge is hand-annotated so breadth is limited.

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

note: Kept from the second pass. No earlier deployed open-domain question answerer was found (Protosynthex was a research system). Ask Jeeves 1996 is later and matched questions to pages. No contemporary 1993-1995 source found in ia_search3. Checked again: Winston's 1993 AI textbook says Katz invited journalists and scientists at JPL to use START for questions about the Neptune encounter, Voyager and the Solar system (Voyager 2 flyby, August 1989); that is a three-topic demonstration, not broad knowledge, so rejected as an earlier fit. Baseball (1961) and Lunar (1971) answer questions only within one narrow domain.

what: The Actuality Systems Perspecta Spatial 3D volumetric display was integrated with a clinical radiation-therapy planning system (Pinnacle) so that planners could view patient anatomy and beams in 3D from any side.
fit: A swept-volume display showing changing patient-derived 3-D images in a 25 cm volume viewable from any side, used for its real purpose in treatment planning.

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: volume that is viewable from any side, floating within a translucent dome

sources.publisher: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics (PMC)
sources.title: Application of a 3D volumetric display for radiation therapy treatment planning I: quality assurance procedures
sources.quote: has been integrated with the Pinnacle TPS (Philips Medical Systems, Madison WI), for treatment planning

note: Replaces second pass 1972 (Cross's moving multiplex hologram, an art/exhibit piece). The date is that of the clinical paper; a web search suggests the first Perspecta was delivered to the NIH Clinical Center in January 2004 (AuntMinnie, host blocked) and 2002 sales to universities for research, so real use probably began about 2002-2004, but I could not fetch a dated source. No earlier use outside the lab found for ITT's 1960 rotating-screen display (only a working model) or Withey's Peritron. Zebra Imaging's printed holographic maps for the US military are static, so excluded. Rechecked: web search found AuntMinnie 19 Jan 2004 (NIH Clinical Center got the first Perspecta, for research) and a BusinessWire release of 30 Nov 2004 (Rush radiation oncology, research into planning); neither page could be fetched here, so no earlier citable use.

what: Kurzweil Applied Intelligence officially released its 1,000-word Voicerad system in Boston in December 1986; a radiologist was already writing his reports with it by voice. Dragon Systems had announced Voicescribe-1000 'automatic dictation transcription system' in June 1986.
fit: A computer listens to a user's spoken dictation of reports and produces the edited, printed text, used by a working radiologist.

sources.title: Voice system cures MD ills
sources.quote: allows radiologists to dictate, edit and print out diagnostic X-ray reports by voice

sources.title: Speech transcriber announced
sources.quote: announced Voicescribe-1000, an automatic dictation transcription system

note: Replaces Dragon Dictate 1990 in the second pass: Kurzweil Voicerad and Dragon Voicescribe-1000 were dictation products in 1986 (PC Magazine 27 Oct 1987 also lists both). Earlier: Threshold Technology voice input from 1972 was data entry of commands, not dictation; Kurzweil 1985 Voice Report not found in searches. Voicescribe-1000 was only announced in June 1986 (availability not shown), so Voicerad December 1986 is the first documented in use. Limited vocabulary and discrete speech, so a strict dictation fit but narrow. Rechecked: Kurzweil's Sept 1985 BYTE item announces a continuous-speech 1000-word board for OEMs, Computerworld Dec 1985 lists Kurzweil and TI as speech-recognition front-runners and calls Dragon's 2,000-word dictation system a prototype; no 1985 dictation system in use by a customer was found.

what: Furby went on general sale in the United States (launched 2 October 1998, with a press event at FAO Schwarz, New York), selling 1.8 million in 1998.
fit: The robotic pet toy was bought and kept by ordinary families as a companion that responds to touch and sound.

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: for his grand arrival at the flagship FAO Schwarz store in early October

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: The product officially launched on October 2, 1998

sources.title: 1998-10-15 W5YI Report
sources.quote: Your kids will be wanting the new interactive Furby “animatronic” toy this Christmas!

note: Replaces second pass 1999-06-01 (AIBO sale; Sony's robot dog went on sale 1999-06-01, 3,000 units in Japan sold out in 20 minutes per a 1999-06-04 news item) because Furby was on sale eight months earlier. Same fit caveat as the demonstration. Paro handmade sales from 2004 are later. Rechecked: Teddy Ruxpin (1985) is a tape-playback animatronic bear with no sensors or response to the child, Tamagotchi (1996) is not a robot; neither fits as a robot companion.

what: Volvo Kalmar assembly plant in regular production use of its fleet of computer-guided carriers.
fit: The plant's fleet of computer-guided carriers did its production work, and all of them could be directed from one central computer.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: forms of "carriers," battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

sources.title: Volvo
sources.quote: carriers at Kalmar can be controlled from a central data computer which is the heart and brain of the factory

note: Same event as the demonstration, so same date. Replaces Walgreens/Kiva 2007. Fit is partial (computer-guided fleet; central control inferred). Rechecked: searched for computer-run AGV/robot fleets before 1974 and found none documented; the 1962 to 1973 hits were unrelated.

what: By 1994 facial-recognition biometric products had reached the marketplace (access control); the DMV offices of West Virginia and New Mexico followed, using automated face recognition against duplicate licences after the 1993 FERET test.
fit: Commercial systems used cameras and computers to match a person's face against an enrolled stored image for entry control and identity checks.

sources.title: Biometric Identification Verification Technology Status and Feasibility Study
sources.quote: Systems which have reached the marketplace include fingerprint, thumbprint, hand geometry, keystroke dynamics, signature dynamics, voice patterns, retina patterns, and facial recognition.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: became the first DMV offices to use automated facial recognition systems to prevent people from obtaining multiple driving licenses

note: Replaces second pass 1997 (ZN-Face sale). The 1994 DTIC study says facial recognition products were already on the market but names no deployment and calls them unreliable (it judged them unable to meet DoD needs), so the date is the earliest documented market presence, not a documented first user. The DMV use (West Virginia, New Mexico) is after 1993 but I found no dated source. Mexico 2000 and Super Bowl 2001 are later. Rechecked: searched Computerworld and InfoWorld 1985-1994 for face recognition and found nothing; AFIT's 1985 Face Recognition Machine was a research prototype.

what: Lawrence LeShan (College of William and Mary) played a phonograph record of 'My finger nails taste terribly bitter' to 20 sleeping boy nail-biters at a summer camp on 54 successive nights; 8 stopped biting their nails and none of the 20 controls changed.
fit: A recording was played to sleeping people and taught them a new response (stopping a habit) that persisted after waking, compared with controls; it is suggestion rather than a lesson of facts, and the last weeks were given by voice after the phonograph failed.

sources.publisher: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
sources.title: The Breaking of a Habit by Suggestion During Sleep (LeShan)
sources.quote: a portable electric phonograph was used with a record made especially for the experiment

sources.publisher: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
sources.title: The Breaking of a Habit by Suggestion During Sleep (LeShan)
sources.quote: This experiment, although somewhat laborious, shows it is possible to give suggestion during sleep.

note: Replaces Zust 2019. LeShan 1942 is a controlled study with the mechanism in the definition (recorded verbal content played during sleep), and the author concluded it shows suggestion during sleep is possible. Weak: small, unblinded to the experimenter, and the habit change was a suggestion not a lesson. Earlier items rejected: Thurstone's wartime Morse-code phonograph trial (abandoned without results, mentioned in the same paper), Saliger's Psycho-Phone (1927, no evidence it worked), Fox and Robbin 1952 and Emmons and Simon 1956 (no recall of material played in sleep).

what: The same Sony Data Discman DD-1 went on sale in Japan in July 1990 as an 'electronic book' player for reference works.
fit: A pocket-size battery device with its own LCD that shows the text of books and reference works stored on a 3-inch CD, replacing paper.

sources.publisher: Daily Universe (Brigham Young University), Associated Press report
sources.title: Electronic book to be marketed
sources.quote: Sony said it plans to begin market- ing the machine in Japan on July 1 for about $380.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

note: Searched for earlier handheld devices that show the text of books. Franklin's 1986 handheld and Japanese pocket electronic dictionaries of the 1980s hold a single dictionary, one line at a time, and no contemporary report calls them an electronic book; they are reference lookup tools, not book readers, so rejected. Yevick 1972, Dynabook 1968-72, Brown 1930 and Hart 1971 were proposals or needed a mainframe. The Data Discman is the first device sold as an 'electronic book' player (AP report of May 1990: palm-sized, shows text of 3-inch discs, sale in Japan July 1). The exact on-sale day is taken from the announcement, not from a sales report.

what: Threshold Technology (Delran/Cinnaminson, NJ) brought out the VIP-100 isolated-word recognizer and had voice-input terminals working in industrial, government and military 'real-world' use from late 1972.
fit: Spoken words were recognized by a commercial machine and used to enter data and give commands to a computer in working environments, outside the laboratory.

sources.publisher: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.title: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.quote: A respectable product was brought out this year by Threshold Technology, Inc.

sources.title: Real-time interactive speech technology at Threshold Technology, Incorporated
sources.quote: Threshold Technology has had voice input systems operating in these "real-world" environments since late 1972

note: Replaces the 1984 Apricot Portable. The same ERIC history says 'No commercially successful ASR device of any consequence has been developed in all these years' before Threshold's 1972 product, which supports 1972 as the first; Computerworld 1972-05-31 reports Threshold's lab demonstration of word input. Not checked: the exact first customer installation (1972-73), the earlier IBM Shoebox (1962, demonstration only) and Japanese NEC systems. A 1972 date rests on the 1977 company paper for deployment plus the contemporary product announcement. Second check: IA full-text searches 1962-1972 for earlier deployed voice-input systems (parcel sorting, inspection, military) found only research or proposals; the Threshold 1972 product is the earliest commercial deployment found. Quotes re-checked FOUND.

what: Clark L. Hull and H. D. Baernstein (Yale) built an electrochemical machine (polarizable cells and mercury-toluene thermal regulators, switches as receptors, a flashlight bulb as responder) that acquired conditioned responses from the sequence of stimuli it received, reported in Science, 5 July 1929.
fit: The machine changed its response from the experience of paired stimuli (a neutral switch came to light the bulb after training, with extinction, forgetting and spontaneous recovery) instead of being wired for that response.

sources.title: A Mechanical Parallel to the Conditioned Reflex
sources.quote: Thus far the following condi- tioned-reflex phenomena have been duplicated

sources.title: A Mechanical Parallel to the Conditioned Reflex
sources.quote: The mechanism which has given the best results is a combination of polarizable cells and mercury- toluene regulators

note: Replaces Shannon's Theseus (1950). Hull and Baernstein's working conditioning machine was published in 1929, and Hull built a related one with Krueger (named in Scientific American, April 1933, which also describes Thomas Ross's 1933 maze-learning machine with relay memory cells; Ross is later than Hull-Baernstein and was not used). The Science note lists the phenomena the machine reproduced (acquisition, extinction, reinforcement, spontaneous recovery, and so on). It is associative learning rather than task-performance improvement on a benchmark, so confidence is medium. Not found: any earlier working learning machine; Stephens 1929 (cited in Psychological Bulletin 1931) was not read and is no earlier than mid-1929.

what: Denning Mobile Robotics' Sentry, marketed as an autonomous mobile security robot guard patrolling warehouses; prison units ordered by Southern Steel (600 ordered, 8 in advanced testing in late 1985).
fit: A robot that patrols facilities on its own and alerts authorities to intruders, sold to customers for real guard duty.

sources.title: Raising a new generation of robots
sources.quote: mobile se curity robot guard works in: dependently patrolling warehouses and other facilities

sources.title: Denning Sentry robot article
sources.quote: eight of these, destined for prison duty, are now undergoing ad- vanced testing

note: Replaces 2015 Knightscope: Denning Sentry (1985-86) was earlier. The exact first customer patrol deployment date was not found (1985 sources say testing/orders; Dec 1985 Robotics Age lists it as a product). Date 1986 is the earliest source describing it as working patrol service. RoboGuard/Prowler not checked. Second check: Quasar Industries' 'security robot' (1979-82 books) and Century 1 (1980, planned) were promotional or planned, with no deployed patrol found; Robot Defense Systems' Prowler was an experimental military sentry; so Denning stays the earliest in service. Quotes re-checked FOUND.

what: Line Material Industries (McGraw-Edison) used the IBM 357 data collection system in which each employee inserts his identification card at a station, the machine records who he is and his time and attendance.
fit: A machine reads each employee's ID card in daily factory use to identify him and record attendance and production against his name.

sources.title: American Machinist 1961-09-18: Vol 105 Iss 19
sources.quote: Each employee inserts his identification card in the 357 station nearest his job loca- tion

note: The ad of Sept 1961 shows a customer in use; a first use in late 1960 is likely but I found no earlier customer report. The second pass's 1968 RIT VALI-DINE (punched-hole cards admitting students to a dining hall) is later but is the earliest access-control use I found. Second check: IBM announced the 357 plastic-badge reader in Oct 1960 (Steel/Industry Week 1960-10-03), so a badge in service before 1961 is unlikely; earlier 357 installations (McDonnell Aircraft, 1959-60) read a prepunched job card, not a person's ID. Embossed charge plates and time-clock cards were not machine-read identity tokens for access or ID checking. No earlier machine-read employee ID found.

what: Thirion, Duchesnay, Hubbard, Dubois, Poline, Lebihan and Dehaene (NeuroSpin, France) decoded fMRI activity to reconstruct the visual pattern that subjects were only imagining, using inverse retinotopy and supervised classifiers (NeuroImage 33(4), 2006).
fit: From brain activity alone, the machine reconstructed an image the person was holding in mind (a mental image, not a displayed stimulus), shown as a reconstructed pattern; the images were crude flickering-pattern shapes.

sources.title: Inverse retinotopy: Inferring the visual content of images from brain activation patterns
sources.quote: in five data sets, our algorithms could reconstruct and predict with significant accuracy a pattern imagined by the subjects

sources.title: Inverse retinotopy: Inferring the visual content of images from brain activation patterns
sources.quote: we use the well-known retinotopy of the visual cortex to infer the visual content of real or imaginary scenes from the brain activation patterns that they elicit

note: Replaces Tang et al. 2023. The definition covers text of thoughts OR mental images/dreams on a screen. Thirion 2006 reconstructs an imagined pattern from fMRI, earlier than the 2023 language decoder; it is crude (a self-chosen pattern from a small set of flickering stimuli), so confidence is low. Rejected as earlier candidates: Farwell and Donchin 1988 P300 speller and Birbaumer 1999 slow-cortical-potential speller (the user picks letters by attention or cursor control; this is selection, not reading out thought content); Vidal 1973 (cursor); Miyawaki 2008 and Nishimoto 2011 (reconstruct images being viewed, not mental images); Horikawa 2013 dream decoding (word categories only); Willett 2021 and Moses 2021 (attempted handwriting or speech); Makin 2020 (spoken sentences). Tang 2023 (PMC11304553, FOUND) is the first decoder of open-ended silent thought into word sequences, the best fit if the checker prefers the text reading of the definition.
